Published online:
    11 September 2026

Geographic focus:
    Strait of Hormuz (Persian Gulf / Middle East), Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb, broader global LNG/commodity shipping corridors

Temporal focus:
    T1. Historical report [YES] — reports on vessel movements and events from early-to-mid September 2026
    T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — ongoing Iran war, U.S. blockade, Houthi advances, and severely depressed Hormuz traffic all point to persisting near-term supply disruption risks
    T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [NO] — no structural or multi-year outlook provided

Synopsis:
    Vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz have collapsed to single digits (7 on the reported day vs. a 10-day average of 15 and a pre-war norm of ~125/day), reflecting the severe disruption caused by the Iran war that began February 28. A U.S. blockade has halted Iranian crude exports since mid-July. LNG flows from Qatar via Hormuz show tentative signs of resumption — one QatarEnergy tanker completed the first known LNG delivery since late July, and two other QE-linked vessels reappeared inside the strait. Simultaneously, Houthi forces seized Yemen's Mocha port and advanced toward Red Sea islands, though Bab el-Mandeb traffic (26 vessels) remains near its 10-day average. The two choke points together represent a critical pinch on global energy supply chains.

Relevance: YES — Hormuz handles ~20% of global LNG supply; traffic is down ~94% vs. pre-war norms; the Qatar LNG resumption is minimal and fragile

Relevance: IMPLICIT — Europe depends materially on Qatari LNG imports; a sustained near-blockade of Hormuz directly tightens European LNG availability, particularly relevant heading into the winter refill season. The article does not mention Europe explicitly, but the supply chain implications are direct.
